title: Two Sum
shortSummary: Use a hash map to find a complement in one pass.
description: Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return indices of the two numbers such that they add up to target.
exampleExplanation: nums[0] + nums[1] equals 9, so return those indices.

solution.intuition: Store each value as you scan so you can instantly check whether the needed complement already appeared.
steps: Create an empty dictionary from number to index.
Loop through nums with index i.
Compute complement = target - nums[i].
If complement exists in the dictionary, return that stored index and i.
Otherwise store nums[i] with index i.
solution.whyOptimal: Every element is visited once and each lookup is constant time on average.
commonMistakes: Adding the current number before checking the complement can reuse the same index.
Forgetting duplicate values can overwrite the needed earlier index.
solution.interviewTip: State the brute force O(n^2) idea first, then explain why hashing removes the nested loop.

title: Valid Parentheses
shortSummary: Match every closing bracket with the latest unmatched opener.
description: Given a string s containing just the characters (), {}, and [], determine if the input string is valid.
exampleExplanation: Each opener is closed in the correct order.
constraints: s consists only of parentheses characters.

solution.intuition: Only the most recent unmatched opener can be closed next, which is exactly stack behavior.
steps: Create a stack and a mapping from closing to opening bracket.
Scan each character.
Push opening brackets onto the stack.
For a closing bracket, ensure the stack is not empty and the top matches.
Return true only if the stack is empty at the end.
solution.whyOptimal: A single pass is enough because each bracket is pushed and popped at most once.
commonMistakes: Not checking for an empty stack before popping.
Ignoring extra opening brackets remaining after the scan.
solution.interviewTip: Mention that order matters, which is why counting brackets alone is insufficient.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
shortSummary: Track the cheapest price so far and the best profit seen.
description: You are given an array prices where prices[i] is the price of a given stock on the i-th day. Maximize profit from one buy and one sell.
exampleExplanation: Buy at 1 and sell at 6 for a profit of 5.

solution.intuition: The best sell today depends on the lowest price seen before today.
steps: Initialize minPrice to a large value and maxProfit to 0.
Iterate through prices.
Update minPrice with the current price if it is smaller.
Otherwise compute current profit = price - minPrice and update maxProfit.
Return maxProfit.
solution.whyOptimal: The algorithm compares each price against the best possible buy before it with no revisits.
commonMistakes: Allowing the sell day before the buy day.
Resetting profit incorrectly after finding a new minimum.
solution.interviewTip: Frame it as maintaining the best state so far rather than trying all pairs.
solution.pythonCode:
def maxProfit(prices):
    min_price = float('inf')
    max_profit = 0
    for price in prices:
        min_price = min(min_price, price)
        max_profit = max(max_profit, price - min_price)
    return max_profit

title: Contains Duplicate
shortSummary: A set reveals repeated values immediately.
description: Given an integer array nums, return true if any value appears at least twice.
exampleExplanation: The value 1 appears more than once.

solution.intuition: If a number is already in the set, it has appeared before.
steps: Create an empty set.
Scan the array.
If the current number is in the set, return true.
Otherwise insert it into the set.
Return false after the loop ends.
solution.whyOptimal: It stops early on the first duplicate and uses constant-time average membership checks.
commonMistakes: Sorting first adds unnecessary O(n log n) time for this version.
Forgetting that negative numbers are still valid set keys.
solution.interviewTip: Use this problem to show you recognize when a set is enough instead of a full map.

title: Product of Array Except Self
shortSummary: Build prefix and suffix products without division.
description: Given an integer array nums, return an array answer such that answer[i] is the product of all elements except nums[i].
exampleExplanation: Each index uses the product of all numbers to its left and right.
constraints: The product of any prefix or suffix fits in a 32-bit integer.

solution.intuition: For each index, multiply everything before it by everything after it.
steps: Create an output array filled with 1s.
Fill output[i] with the prefix product before i.
Track a running suffix product from right to left.
Multiply each output[i] by the suffix product after i.
Return the output array.
solution.whyOptimal: It achieves the no-division requirement while using the output array as storage.
commonMistakes: Using division breaks when zeros appear.
Allocating separate prefix and suffix arrays when the prompt asks for constant extra space.
solution.interviewTip: Clarify whether the output array counts toward space complexity, because interviewers usually exclude it.
solution.pythonCode:
def productExceptSelf(nums):
    result = [1] * len(nums)
    prefix = 1
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        result[i] = prefix
        prefix *= nums[i]
    suffix = 1
    for i in range(len(nums) - 1, -1, -1):
        result[i] *= suffix
        suffix *= nums[i]
    return result

title: Maximum Subarray
shortSummary: Keep the best subarray ending here and the best overall.
description: Given an integer array nums, find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum and return its sum.
exampleExplanation: The subarray [4,-1,2,1] has the largest sum of 6.

solution.intuition: A negative running sum only hurts future subarrays, so restart when needed.
steps: Initialize currentSum and bestSum with the first value.
For each next number, decide whether to start fresh or extend the current subarray.
Update currentSum with max(num, currentSum + num).
Update bestSum with max(bestSum, currentSum).
Return bestSum.
solution.whyOptimal: Each element contributes once to the running state, so no nested scans are needed.
commonMistakes: Resetting current sum to zero fails when all values are negative.
Losing track of the best overall answer while updating the running sum.
solution.interviewTip: Explain the state transition in words before writing the compact formula.

title: Binary Search
shortSummary: Shrink the sorted search space by half each step.
description: Given a sorted array of integers nums and a target value, return its index or -1 if not found.
exampleExplanation: The target 9 exists at index 4.
constraints: All integers in nums are unique and sorted in ascending order.

solution.intuition: Sorted order tells you which half cannot contain the target.
steps: Initialize left = 0 and right = nums.count - 1.
While left <= right, compute mid carefully.
If nums[mid] equals target, return mid.
If nums[mid] is too small, move left to mid + 1; otherwise move right to mid - 1.
Return -1 if the loop finishes.
solution.whyOptimal: Each comparison discards half the remaining candidates.
commonMistakes: Using mid = (left + right) / 2 without considering overflow in other languages.
Mixing inclusive and exclusive bounds.
solution.interviewTip: State your interval convention out loud so edge cases stay consistent.

title: Merge Intervals
shortSummary: Sort intervals first so overlaps can be merged greedily.
description: Given an array of intervals where intervals[i] = [starti, endi], merge all overlapping intervals.
exampleExplanation: The first two intervals overlap and become [1,6].

solution.intuition: After sorting by start time, any overlap can only happen with the most recent merged interval.
steps: Sort intervals by starting point.
Initialize the result with the first interval.
For each next interval, compare it with the last merged interval.
If they overlap, extend the last interval's end.
Otherwise append the new interval.
solution.whyOptimal: Sorting organizes the intervals once, then one linear sweep finishes the work.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to sort first.
Comparing with the previous raw interval instead of the latest merged interval.
solution.interviewTip: Say explicitly why sorting turns a global overlap problem into a local decision.

title: Number of Islands
shortSummary: Flood-fill each unvisited land cell to count one island.
description: Given a 2D grid map of '1's and '0's, count the number of islands.
exampleExplanation: There are three disconnected groups of land.

solution.intuition: Once you discover land, traverse its whole connected component so it is only counted once.
steps: Loop through every cell.
When you find unvisited land, increment the island count.
Run DFS or BFS from that cell.
Mark every connected land cell as visited.
Continue scanning the grid.
solution.whyOptimal: Every cell is visited a constant number of times across the whole traversal.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(m * n) in recursion worst case
commonMistakes: Counting diagonal neighbors as connected when only four directions matter.
Forgetting to mark visited cells, causing repeated work.
solution.interviewTip: Tell the interviewer whether you prefer DFS recursion or iterative BFS and mention stack-depth tradeoffs.

title: Clone Graph
shortSummary: Map original nodes to cloned nodes during traversal.
description: Given a reference of a node in a connected undirected graph, return a deep copy of the graph.
exampleOutput: Cloned graph with the same adjacency structure
exampleExplanation: Each original node gets exactly one clone, and neighbor links mirror the input graph.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 100].

solution.intuition: A dictionary prevents duplicate clones and also handles cycles.
steps: Handle the empty graph case.
Create a map from original node value to cloned node.
Run DFS from the starting node.
If a node was already cloned, return the clone immediately.
Otherwise create the clone and recursively clone neighbors.
solution.whyOptimal: Each node and edge is processed once while the map guarantees reuse.
commonMistakes: Creating multiple clones of the same node in cyclic graphs.
Forgetting to connect cloned neighbors.
solution.interviewTip: Point out that the hash map is serving both memoization and cycle detection.

title: Top K Frequent Elements
shortSummary: Count frequencies, then keep the k most common values.
description: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k most frequent elements.
exampleExplanation: 1 appears three times and 2 appears twice, more than any others.
constraints: 1 <= k <= the number of unique elements.

solution.intuition: Frequency counts fit naturally into buckets indexed by occurrence count.
steps: Build a frequency map.
Create buckets where index i stores values seen i times.
Place each number into the bucket matching its frequency.
Iterate buckets from high to low frequency.
Collect values until k answers are gathered.
solution.whyOptimal: Bucket sort avoids the extra log factor of sorting all unique elements by frequency.
commonMistakes: Sorting by numeric value instead of frequency.
Stopping too early when a bucket contains multiple answers.
solution.interviewTip: Offer the heap-based alternative if the interviewer asks about streaming data or very large unique sets.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
shortSummary: Expand a window and move the left edge past duplicates.
description: Given a string s, find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
exampleExplanation: The answer is "abc", with length 3.
constraints: s consists of English letters, digits, symbols, and spaces.

solution.approachName: Sliding Window with Last Seen Index
solution.intuition: When a duplicate appears, only the window section up to its previous index becomes invalid.
steps: Track each character's last seen index in a dictionary.
Maintain a left pointer for the current valid window.
For each right pointer, if the character was seen inside the current window, move left past that old index.
Update the last seen index for the character.
Update the best window length.
solution.whyOptimal: Both pointers only move forward, so the scan stays linear.
commonMistakes: Moving left backward when an old duplicate lies outside the current window.
Using a set-only approach without carefully shrinking multiple times.
solution.interviewTip: Describe the window invariant clearly: all characters between left and right are unique.

title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
shortSummary: Inorder traversal of a BST yields sorted values.
description: Given the root of a binary search tree and an integer k, return the kth smallest value in the tree.
exampleExplanation: The inorder traversal is [1,2,3,4], so the first smallest is 1.
constraints: The number of nodes is n.

solution.intuition: BST ordering guarantees left subtree, node, then right subtree appears in ascending order.
steps: Perform an inorder traversal.
Count nodes as you visit them.
When the count reaches k, record the answer.
Stop early if desired once the answer is found.
Return the stored value.
solution.whyOptimal: You only visit nodes until the kth smallest is reached, with no extra sorting.
commonMistakes: Using preorder or postorder traversal, which does not preserve sorted order.
Forgetting the recursion stack depth in space analysis.
solution.interviewTip: Mention that an augmented BST with subtree sizes can support repeated kth queries faster.

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a BST
shortSummary: Use BST ordering to walk toward the split point.
description: Given a binary search tree, find the lowest common ancestor of two given nodes in the BST.
exampleExplanation: One node lies in the left subtree and the other in the right subtree of 6.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [2, 10^5].

solution.intuition: If both nodes are on the same side, the ancestor must also be on that side.
steps: Start from the root.
If both target values are less than root.val, move left.
If both target values are greater than root.val, move right.
Otherwise the current node is the split point and answer.
Return that node.
solution.whyOptimal: The search follows just one path down the tree.
commonMistakes: Using a general binary tree solution and ignoring BST ordering.
Comparing node identity incorrectly when only values are needed for direction.
solution.interviewTip: Call out that BST structure removes the need to search both subtrees.

title: Meeting Rooms II
shortSummary: Track the earliest finishing meeting while scanning starts.
description: Given an array of meeting time intervals intervals where intervals[i] = [starti, endi], return the minimum number of conference rooms required.
exampleExplanation: The meeting starting at 5 overlaps with the one ending at 30, so two rooms are needed.

solution.intuition: You only need to know which room frees up earliest to decide whether a new room is required.
steps: Sort intervals by start time.
Push the first meeting end time into a min heap.
For each next meeting, compare its start with the earliest end time.
If the earliest meeting ended, reuse that room by popping.
Push the current end time and track the maximum heap size.
solution.whyOptimal: The heap keeps exactly the active meetings, which is the minimum state needed.
commonMistakes: Sorting by end time instead of start time for this approach.
Using heap size at the end instead of tracking the maximum size during processing.
solution.interviewTip: If asked for alternatives, mention the two-sorted-arrays sweep line approach.

title: Coin Change
shortSummary: Build the cheapest way to make every amount up to the target.
description: Given an array of coin denominations and an amount, return the fewest number of coins needed to make up that amount.
exampleExplanation: 11 can be made with 5 + 5 + 1, so the answer is 3.

solution.intuition: The best answer for amount x depends on the best answers for smaller reachable amounts.
steps: Create a dp array of size amount + 1 filled with amount + 1.
Set dp[0] = 0.
For each amount from 1 to target, try every coin.
If coin <= current amount, update dp[current] = min(dp[current], dp[current - coin] + 1).
Return -1 if dp[amount] is still the sentinel value.
solution.whyOptimal: It systematically reuses solved subproblems instead of recomputing combinations.
commonMistakes: Using greedy selection fails for denominations like [1,3,4].
Using an incorrect sentinel can overflow when adding 1.
solution.interviewTip: Lead with the recurrence and base case to show you understand the DP state.

title: Word Break
shortSummary: Mark prefixes that can be formed from dictionary words.
description: Given a string s and a dictionary of strings wordDict, return true if s can be segmented into a space-separated sequence of dictionary words.
exampleExplanation: "leetcode" can be segmented as "leet code".

solution.intuition: If a prefix is breakable and the next chunk is a dictionary word, the longer prefix is also breakable.
steps: Put the dictionary into a set.
Create a dp array where dp[i] means the prefix ending before i is breakable.
Set dp[0] = true for the empty prefix.
For each end index, try all earlier split points.
If dp[start] is true and s[start..<end] is in the set, set dp[end] = true.
solution.whyOptimal: It avoids recomputing the same suffix decisions by caching prefix validity.
commonMistakes: Recursing without memoization causes exponential blowup.
Forgetting the empty-prefix base case.
solution.interviewTip: Explain that dp[i] answers a yes-no question about a prefix, not the number of ways.

title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
shortSummary: Reverse the flow and start DFS/BFS from each ocean edge.
description: Given an m x n matrix of heights, return coordinates where water can flow to both the Pacific and Atlantic oceans.
exampleExplanation: Those cells can reach both oceans following non-increasing water flow paths.

solution.intuition: Instead of flowing outward from every cell, walk inward from each ocean using non-decreasing heights.
steps: Start DFS/BFS from all Pacific-border cells and mark what can reach the Pacific.
Start DFS/BFS from all Atlantic-border cells and mark what can reach the Atlantic.
During traversal, only move to neighbors with height greater than or equal to the current cell.
Intersect the two reachable sets.
Return the intersecting coordinates.
solution.whyOptimal: Each cell is processed at most twice, once per ocean, which is much cheaper than exploring from every cell.
commonMistakes: Following the water direction forward instead of reversing the traversal.
Using strict greater-than and incorrectly blocking equal heights.
solution.interviewTip: Call out the reversal trick early because that is the main insight.

title: Course Schedule
shortSummary: Detect whether the prerequisite graph contains a cycle.
description: There are a total of numCourses courses you have to take, labeled from 0 to numCourses - 1. Determine if it is possible to finish all courses.
exampleExplanation: Take course 0 before course 1, so all courses can be finished.

solution.intuition: If you can repeatedly remove nodes with indegree zero, the graph is acyclic.
steps: Build the adjacency list and indegree counts.
Push all courses with indegree zero into a queue.
Pop from the queue and count completed courses.
Reduce indegrees of dependent courses and enqueue new zero-indegree nodes.
Return whether the completed count equals numCourses.
solution.whyOptimal: Kahn's algorithm resolves cycle detection in one pass over nodes and edges.
commonMistakes: Reversing edge directions and miscomputing indegrees.
Forgetting disconnected courses that start with indegree zero.
solution.interviewTip: Mention that DFS cycle detection is an equally valid alternative if asked.
solution.pythonCode:
from collections import deque

def canFinish(numCourses, prerequisites):
    graph = [[] for _ in range(numCourses)]
    indegree = [0] * numCourses
    for course, prereq in prerequisites:
        graph[prereq].append(course)
        indegree[course] += 1
    queue = deque(i for i, degree in enumerate(indegree) if degree == 0)
    completed = 0
    while queue:
        course = queue.popleft()
        completed += 1
        for neighbor in graph[course]:
            indegree[neighbor] -= 1
            if indegree[neighbor] == 0:
                queue.append(neighbor)
    return completed == numCourses

title: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
shortSummary: Encode structure and values with preorder traversal plus null markers.
description: Design an algorithm to serialize and deserialize a binary tree.
exampleOutput: A codec that reconstructs the same tree
exampleExplanation: Null markers preserve missing child positions so the tree can be rebuilt exactly.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 10^4].

solution.intuition: A tree can be recreated if you record node values in traversal order and explicitly note missing children.
steps: Serialize with preorder traversal.
Append a sentinel such as # for nil nodes.
Join the tokens with commas.
For deserialization, read tokens in preorder.
Rebuild recursively by consuming one token at a time.
solution.whyOptimal: The traversal touches each node once and stores only the information needed to rebuild structure.
commonMistakes: Skipping null markers, which loses tree structure.
Using a shared index incorrectly during deserialization recursion.
solution.interviewTip: State that the exact string format is flexible as long as serialization and deserialization agree.
